recent_posts.title: The Tech Lead Trap
recent_posts.summary: The tech lead role can quietly become a career dead end. Once you've mastered the basics, the work becomes routine and growth stalls invisibly — your manager sees a reliable performer, your team sees a steady leader, but you've stopped learning. Key warning signs include running on autopilot, fading curiosity, and unchanged conversations year over year. Escaping requires intentional action: volunteering for cross-functional work, contributing beyond your team, seeking honest feedback, and confronting uncomfortable skill gaps. Eventually most tech leads face a fork — engineering management or the technical track toward Staff/Principal roles. Staying in the middle without progressing in either direction is itself a trap. Even if you want to stay in the role, rotating to harder teams, setting explicit growth goals, and pursuing deliberate practice can keep stagnation at bay.

recent_posts.title: Inheriting a Struggling Team
recent_posts.summary: Practical guidance for tech leads who inherit a struggling team. Covers how to diagnose root causes through 1:1s and historical review, build trust through consistent small actions, handle performance issues fairly, manage technical debt sustainably, and reset stakeholder relationships. Emphasizes that turnarounds take 6–12 months and require honest communication over optimistic promises.

recent_posts.title: Giving Hard Feedback
recent_posts.summary: A practical guide for tech leads and engineering managers on delivering difficult feedback effectively. Covers core principles (be specific, address behavior not character, act early, keep it private), a structured conversation framework, how to handle common emotional reactions like defensiveness or silence, follow-up practices, and common mistakes to avoid such as the feedback sandwich or vague criticism. Also addresses what to do when feedback doesn't lead to improvement.

recent_posts.title: Making Technical Decisions Stick
recent_posts.summary: Technical decisions fade when they're undocumented, unfindable, or made without involving the right people. The key is matching documentation weight to decision importance: verbal agreement for small reversible choices, written summaries for multi-person decisions, ADRs for architecture-limiting choices, and RFCs for high-stakes decisions needing broad input. A good ADR is a single-page document capturing context, decision, results, and rejected options. RFCs only work when they're genuine invitations for feedback with clear timelines and real follow-through. Keeping ADRs in a /docs/adr folder in the repo, using consistent numbering, and referencing them in code reviews and discussions ensures decisions remain visible and actionable rather than becoming forgotten suggestions.

recent_posts.title: Scope Creep and How to Fight It
recent_posts.summary: Scope creep happens gradually through seemingly reasonable requests that accumulate into timeline-breaking additions. Recognize patterns like "while you're in there" requests and "just a small tweak" additions. Fight it by defining explicit scope boundaries upfront, quantifying impact of changes, forcing trade-off decisions, and using structural approaches like timeboxing and change request processes. Accept legitimate changes driven by new information, but push back on wishful thinking. Make creep visible and trade-offs explicit to build a culture that respects constraints.

recent_posts.title: Sentry AI Tracing with Laravel's AI SDK
recent_posts.summary: Laravel's new official AI SDK simplifies Sentry tracing for LLM calls through event-driven architecture. Instead of manually wrapping each OpenAI call, a single event listener automatically traces all AI interactions—chat completions, streaming, and embeddings—across any provider. The SDK fires events with invocation IDs that correlate start and finish spans, handling token counts and metadata automatically. The listener approach eliminates the need to remember tracing wrappers while maintaining the same gen_ai.* attribute conventions for Sentry's LLM monitoring UI.

recent_posts.title: How tech leads should say no to protect team capacity
recent_posts.summary: Saying no is a critical skill for tech leads to protect team capacity and delivery quality. The article explains when to push back (when value doesn't justify cost, quality will suffer, team is overloaded, better solutions exist, or conflicts with priorities), how to do it effectively through problem-solving language rather than rejection, and how to adapt the approach for different stakeholders. Building credibility through consistent reasoning, reliable execution, and strategic yes's makes your no's more effective. While you'll sometimes be wrong, saying yes to everything guarantees worse outcomes through burnout and declining quality.

recent_posts.title: Managing Up
recent_posts.summary: Tech leads must proactively share information with their engineering managers to enable good decisions. Effective managing up means providing regular updates on risks, blockers, team health, and progress with specific details rather than vague statements. When advocating for team needs, connect requests to business outcomes and provide options rather than just problems. Build influence through credibility and make decisions easy by doing upfront work. Common mistakes include assuming managers know about issues, waiting too long to share bad news, and only communicating when needing something.

recent_posts.title: Working with Designers
recent_posts.summary: Tech leads and designers optimize for different goals, creating natural tension that requires active management rather than resolution. Success comes from early collaboration during problem definition, not after designs are finalized. When pushback is necessary, focus on understanding intent, explaining costs transparently, and offering alternatives. The "pixel perfect" debate requires explicit prioritization of what matters versus what doesn't. Building strong designer relationships involves learning their tools, sharing yours, and treating design as an equal partner in the product trio alongside product management.

recent_posts.title: Working with Product Managers
recent_posts.summary: The tech lead and product manager relationship works best as a partnership where both own outcomes together, not as a handoff between spec-writer and implementer. Success requires early involvement in problem definition, mutual influence on decisions, shared ownership of results, and regular communication to build trust. Tech leads should learn the product context, share technical constraints early, ask why behind requests, and offer alternatives when pushing back. Common failures include adversarial dynamics, absent PMs, spec-following tech leads, and scope creep. The foundation is both parties solving the same problem rather than protecting territory.
